solution:
Suppose, if possible, that \(4\sqrt{2}\) is a rational number. Then \(4\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q}\) for some integers \(p, q\) with \(q \ne 0\).
Dividing both sides by \(4\), \(\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{4q}\). Here \(p\) and \(4q\) are integers and \(4q \ne 0\), so \(\frac{p}{4q}\) is a rational number, which means \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational.
But \(\sqrt{2}\) is known to be irrational. This is a contradiction, so our supposition is false.
Hence \(4\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.

Suppose, if possible, that \(3+\sqrt{5}\) is a rational number. Then \(3+\sqrt{5} = \frac{p}{q}\) for some integers \(p, q\) with \(q \ne 0\).
Subtracting \(3\) from both sides, \(\sqrt{5} = \frac{p}{q} - 3 = \frac{p-3q}{q}\). Here \(p-3q\) and \(q\) are integers and \(q \ne 0\), so \(\sqrt{5}\) would be a rational number.
But \(\sqrt{5}\) is known to be irrational. This is a contradiction, so our supposition is false.
Hence \(3+\sqrt{5}\) is an irrational number.

Each surd is written as the hypotenuse of a right triangle with whole-number legs, and that length is then swung back onto the number line with a compass.
For \(\sqrt{5}\): note \(5 = 2^{2}+1^{2}\). On the number line take \(O\) at \(0\) and \(A\) at \(2\). At \(A\) draw \(AB\) perpendicular to the number line with \(AB = 1\) unit. In right triangle \(OAB\), \(OB = \sqrt{OA^{2}+AB^{2}} = \sqrt{2^{2}+1^{2}} = \sqrt{5}\). With centre \(O\) and radius \(OB\), draw an arc cutting the number line at \(C\); then \(C\) represents \(\sqrt{5}\).
For \(\sqrt{10}\): note \(10 = 3^{2}+1^{2}\). Take \(P\) at \(3\) on the number line and draw \(PQ\) perpendicular to it with \(PQ = 1\) unit. In right triangle \(OPQ\), \(OQ = \sqrt{3^{2}+1^{2}} = \sqrt{10}\). With centre \(O\) and radius \(OQ\), draw an arc cutting the number line at \(D\); then \(D\) represents \(\sqrt{10}\).
The points \(C\) and \(D\) so obtained represent \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(\sqrt{10}\) on the number line, lying between \(2\) and \(3\) and between \(3\) and \(4\) respectively.

Show the two compass arcs centred at O sweeping OB and OQ down onto the line, meeting it at C (between 2 and 3) and D (between 3 and 4), labelled sqrt5 and sqrt10.

The numbers must lie between \(-0.5\) and \(0.3\), that is \(-0.5 < x < 0.3\). Any decimals in this range will do, and there are infinitely many of them.
\(-0.4,\ -0.3,\ 0.2\)

Since \(-2.33 < -2.3\), the numbers must satisfy \(-2.33 < x < -2.30\). Writing both endpoints to three decimal places, \(-2.330\) and \(-2.300\), makes the choices easy; there are infinitely many such numbers.
\(-2.310,\ -2.320,\ -2.325\)

The numbers must satisfy \(5.2 < x < 5.3\). Writing the endpoints as \(5.20\) and \(5.30\), any two-decimal number between them will do, and there are infinitely many of them.
\(5.21,\ 5.22,\ 5.23\)

Since \(-4.6 < -4.5\), the numbers must satisfy \(-4.60 < x < -4.50\). Any two-decimal number between these will do, and there are infinitely many of them.
\(-4.51,\ -4.55,\ -4.58\)
